question: Does a defender’s energy management before an attack predict being passed?
hidden_fact: F1 does not publish battery or active-aero data for 2026. Everything here is estimated from public speed, throttle and position telemetry, under stated assumptions.
verdict_sentence: An earlier cut-off on the approach straight did not predict being passed. Pace difference and Overtake availability did.
caveat: “No effect” means none detectable with this estimator and sample, not proof of absence. The test covers only passes whose approach straight carried a detectable defender cut-off.

terms.deploy_rel_diff: Relative deploy energy, defender minus attacker
terms.pace_delta: Pace delta (attacker minus defender lap time)

spot_checks.detail: Main-straight cut-off not far earlier than his median (+51, +63, −41, −10, −65 m); lap 51 is 1.9 std, below the 2 std bar.
Hamilton’s cut-off on lap 62 is earlier (−55 m), not later; Verstappen within noise.

spot_checks.moment: Ferrari earlier than Mercedes at Monza
spot_checks.detail: Straight 2 matches in direction but intervals overlap Antonelli’s by 2 m; straight 4 is opposite; Leclerc retired early.

spot_checks.moment: Piastri, harvest limit at Monza vs Baku

limits: No public battery data exists; spot checks are the only external anchors, and three of four testable ones failed.
A session-wide value is used and sits at a grid bound in 16 of 45 sessions; relative deploy energy inherits this.
3.7 Hz telemetry with integer speeds: cut-off distances carry tens of metres of lap-to-lap scatter.
Only passes whose approach straight has a detected defender cut-off on the previous lap enter the test.
Per-event energy limits for races are not public; the 100 kW/s derate rate is an assumption.
Hungary is excluded (D17); Sakhir and Jeddah have no usable data.
